answersA.text: Blocks are a fundamental feature in Ruby, providing a way to group code that can be passed to methods. Blocks are implicitly associated with the method they are passed to and can be accessed within that method using the `yield` keyword.

answersA.title: Swift optionals explained
answersA.text: Optionals in Swift are a way to handle the absence of a value. They are represented by a type followed by a question mark, like `String?`. This indicates that the variable can either hold a value of that type, or it can be `nil`, meaning it holds no value. You must safely unwrap an optional before you can use its value, typically using `if let` or `guard let` statements to check if it contains a value.

answersA.title: Compare Java 8, 11, 17, and 21
answersA.text: The Java Development Kit has seen significant updates since version 8. Java 11 introduced features like the `var` keyword for local variable type inference and new methods in the String API. Java 17 brought LTS (Long-Term Support) status, along with pattern matching for `switch` and sealed classes. Most recently, Java 21, also an LTS release, offers further enhancements such as virtual threads for improved concurrency and pattern matching for records.

newInput: How does caching work in Redis?

answersA.title: How caching works in Redis
answersA.text: Caching in Redis works by storing frequently accessed data in memory for quick retrieval. When a request comes in, Redis first checks its in-memory cache. If the data is found (a cache hit), it's returned immediately, which is very fast. If the data is not in the cache (a cache miss), Redis retrieves it from the primary data store, returns it to the client, and then stores a copy in its cache for future requests. This significantly reduces latency and database load.

answersA.title: How Redis caching works
answersA.text: Caching in Redis works by storing frequently accessed data in memory, which allows for much faster retrieval than traditional disk-based databases. When an application needs data, it first checks Redis. If the data is found (a cache hit), it's returned immediately. If not (a cache miss), the application fetches the data from the primary data store, sends it to the client, and also stores a copy in Redis for future requests. This reduces load on the primary database and speeds up response times.

answersA.title: Redis eviction policies
answersA.text: Redis eviction policies determine which keys are removed from the cache when memory is full. Common policies include LRU (Least Recently Used), LFU (Least Frequently Used), TTL (Time To Live), and random eviction. LRU removes keys that haven't been accessed for the longest time. LFU removes keys that have been accessed the fewest times. TTL removes keys that have expired based on their set expiration time. Random eviction simply removes a random key. Choosing the right policy depends on your application's access patterns.

Common policies include LRU (Least Recently Used), LFU (Least Frequently Used), TTL (Time To Live), or random selection. These policies help maintain performance by ensuring that the most relevant data remains in the cache.

answersA.title: Redis eviction policies
answersA.text: Redis eviction policies determine which keys are removed from the cache when it reaches its memory limit. Common policies include LRU (Least Recently Used), which removes the least recently accessed keys, and LFU (Least Frequently Used), which removes the least frequently accessed keys. Other options include random eviction or a combination of policies. The choice depends on the specific access patterns of your application.
